text.tspan: 2 Peter Sources
Jude: Who Used Who?
Returning to Matthews’ article
, he uses
CT to test the consensus
that 2 Peter used Jude.
He gives examples of
the arguments scholars
use for the Synoptic Problem I just described in the previous
paragraph.
He says, “If these kinds of grammatical corrections argue
so strongly for Markan priority [that Mark was the first gospel written
due in part because of its
rougher Greek in comparison with the other
Gospels
, what does this have to say about 2 Peter and Jude? Any
student of 2 Peter is aware of its poor grammar and style in relation to
Jude’s relatively good Greek, polished style and tight structure.”
And
later, “Thus, the consensus in modern scholarship, especially as regards
grammarians, is that 2 Peter employs poor Greek grammar and style.
This is especially true in relation to the epistle of Jude.”
Matthew
helpful states, “One can posit reasons why one author may rework
material to suit his own purposes, but to suppose that one another would
deliberately change good grammar to bad is far less plausible.”
The
passages he uses to argue his case are
2 Peter 2:4
10a with Jude 5
Peter 2:12
13a with Jude 10,
2 Peter 2:13b with Jude 12a, and
2 Peter
3 with Jude 17
His conclusion: “If the argument from grammar
holds true in favour of Markan priority, the evidence put forth here
makes it possible to suggest that 2 Peter is also prior.”
This is not the only theory scholars have proposed. Bauckham
notes four explanations for 2 Peter and Jude’s
literary relationship: (1)
Jude used 2 Peter, (2) 2 Peter used Jude, (3) both used a common
source, or
(4) both letters were written by the same individual.
(1) We have already examined this explanation.
(2) We
will examine this view in a moment.
. He does not call use “CT” in his article. This is a term I have employed for clarity.
. See M. Matthews, “The Literary Relationship of 2 Peter and Jude,” 48
50. He says, “These
examples represent only a few of the many instances in which Matthew and Luke have
improved
Mark’s poor grammar and style” (p. 50).
. M. Matthew, “The Literary Relationship of 2 Peter and Jude,” 50.
. M. Matthews, “The Literary Relationship of 2 Peter and Jude,” 51.
While Bauckham notes
2 Peter uses an “Asiatic” style, Matthew counters, “‘Asianism’ was not so much a style as it was a
p
ejorative term for Greek Hellenistic writing that showed a lack of restraint or inability to use
sententious phrases” (p. 51).
Note
also that Bauckham says, “Second Peter’s style is so consistent
that its author must in any case have rewritten his source fairly freely.” See R. Bauckham,
Jude, 2
Peter
